name: Families, Heritage Speakers, and Home Languages
title: Families, Heritage Speakers, and Home Languages
answer: English learners' families are partners in their education, and home language support lets a parent help a child even without strong English. Heritage speakers, who grew up speaking a language at home, can build reading and writing skills in that language through AI activities pitched at the right level. Schools should treat these language skills as an asset rather than a problem to be managed.

sections.body: Families of English learners often want to help with schoolwork but are shut out when everything arrives in English. This idea treats the home language as a working tool rather than an obstacle, so a parent can give homework help in the language they know best. Teachers can send instructions and tips in the family's language through TalkingPoints, which translates messages in both directions. Heritage speakers are students who grew up speaking a language at home, and some speak English well while still wanting to build literacy in their home language. The problem it solves is a school that values only English, which cuts families out of the work and leaves a student's existing language skills unused.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher sends homework instructions and tips to families in their own language through TalkingPoints, which translates messages both ways, so a parent can support a child without strong English. For heritage speakers, a teacher can use AI to create reading and writing activities in the home language at the right level, which serves both students still learning English and students who speak English well but want to grow their home language literacy. Teachers looking for culturally responsive materials that reflect students' backgrounds can search library databases and AI tools, then check what they find for accuracy and respect. The text does not set out separate practices by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: A review of 94 publications found that using students' home languages helped them learn content, and that monolingual norms in schools were a barrier (Moraru, 2025). That is the finding the text reports, and it is the only research it cites for this idea. The text does not attach a formal evidence label to it, so the claim rests on that review rather than on a stated tier. The rest of the idea, including the use of TalkingPoints and AI to create home language activities, is described as practice rather than as something a study tested.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Two limits stand out. Materials found through library databases and AI tools still have to be checked for accuracy and respect before they reach students, and that check is a person's job, not the tool's. The text also warns that monolingual norms in schools are a barrier, which means the idea only works if a school genuinely treats home languages as an asset rather than tolerating them. Decisions about what a family receives in its own language, and what level of home language work suits a particular student, stay with the teacher and the family. Nothing here is legal advice, and the text sets out practice rather than requirements.
